_sources.usda: USDA FoodData Central, https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/ (record named in each entry), read 2026-10-27
_sources.nihOds: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements fact sheets (Iron, Folate, Vitamin C, Vitamin K, Magnesium, Zinc, Potassium, Vitamin A, Calcium, Vitamin B12, Vitamin D, Vitamin E), https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/list-all/; reference intakes as listed in build_draft_batch.py (RDA for adult women)
_sources.niddk: NIDDK, Eating, Diet & Nutrition for Kidney Stones, read 2026-10-26: nuts and nut products, peanuts, rhubarb, spinach and wheat bran listed among foods to reduce for calcium oxalate stones

catfish.desc: Fish, catfish, channel, farmed, cooked, dry heat
catfish.how: Bake, grill or pan-fry fillets; a light coating of cornmeal or spices works well.
catfish.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
catfish.reviewNote: Farmed channel catfish, the type sold in the US. Wild and imported catfish differ.
catfish.name: Catfish

lobster.desc: Crustaceans, lobster, northern, cooked, moist heat
lobster.how: Steam or boil, then eat the meat with lemon, or add it to salads and pasta.
lobster.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
lobster.name: Lobster

octopus.desc: Mollusks, octopus, common, cooked, moist heat
octopus.how: Simmer slowly until tender, then slice for salads or grill briefly.
octopus.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
octopus.reviewNote: The USDA record shows 36 µg of vitamin B12 per 100 g, about fifteen times the adult reference intake in one serving. It is the figure USDA publishes, but it is unusually high and was flagged for a second look rather than rounded or adjusted.
octopus.name: Octopus

squid.how: Cook quickly over high heat or simmer slowly; in between it turns tough.
squid.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
squid.reviewNote: USDA also has a fried (battered) squid record with more fat and carbohydrate (175 kcal per 85 g); the raw record is used here because the catalogue does not say it is fried.
squid.name: Squid

tuna.desc: Fish, tuna, light, canned in water, without salt, drained solids
tuna.state: light tuna, canned in water, no salt, drained
tuna.how: Drain and mix into salads, sandwiches, pasta and grain bowls.
tuna.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
tuna.reviewNote: Canned light tuna, matching the catalogue caution "prefer light/skipjack". Fresh tuna, albacore and bigeye are different records with different mercury levels; this profile does not cover them. Mercury advice for tuna was not looked up for this draft beyond the catalogue caution.
tuna.name: Tuna

herring.desc: Fish, herring, Atlantic, cooked, dry heat
herring.how: Pan-fry or grill fillets, or serve with potatoes and onions.
herring.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
herring.reviewNote: Cooked fresh herring; pickled and smoked herring (common in shops) are different and much saltier.
herring.name: Herring

smoked-salmon.how: Serve on toast or bagels, with eggs, or in salads and pasta.
smoked-salmon.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
smoked-salmon.reviewNote: Cold-smoked chinook (lox). Vitamin D, E and K are not given in the lox record (the other smoked chinook record, 173687, gives vitamin D 17.1 µg per 100 g). It is a salty, cured food (sodium not shown), and the catalogue lists no caution; preparation and pregnancy cautions for smoked fish were not looked up for this draft.
smoked-salmon.name: Smoked salmon
